t: K Highest Ranked Items Within a Price Range — BFS Distance Plus Lexicographic Selection
o: The grid mixes walls (0) with freely walkable cells, and shortest-path distances from start fall straight out of a BFS. Example 1 walks the frontier outward from (0,0): items (0,1), (1,1), (2,1) and (2,2) sit at distances 1–4, so with k = 3 the first three win. Example 2 demonstrates tie-breaking: (2,1) and (1,2) share distance 2, so price decides (2 < 3) before row and column ever matter. Because m·n ≤ 10⁵, a single BFS plus sorting all in-range candidates fits easily; the whole ranking collapses to lexicographic order on the tuple (distance, price, row, column).
k: BFS from start computes shortest distances to every reachable cell in O(mn).
Among cells priced in [low, high], rank is exactly lexicographic order on (distance, price, row, col).
If fewer than k items qualify, return them all — taking a prefix handles this automatically.

a.i: Flood the grid with BFS while recording dist for each visited cell, appending every cell whose price falls inside the range as a candidate keyed by (dist, price, row, col). Sorting that list orders items exactly by rank; slice off the first k coordinates.
s: BFS from start, skipping walls (grid value 0); track visits with dist initialized to −1.
Collect (dist, price, row, col) whenever low ≤ grid[r][c] ≤ high.
Return [row, col] for the first min(k, count) entries.
a.t: O(mn log mn) — BFS is linear and sorting the ≤ mn candidates dominates.
a.sp: O(mn) — distance grid, queue and candidate list.

a.i: Distance ranks increase level by level, so process the BFS frontier one layer at a time: sort the in-price items of the current level by (price, row, col) and append them until k items are gathered. Within a level distance is constant, so the remaining criteria decide; across levels the order is automatic, and everything stops early once k is reached.
s: Maintain the current frontier and a seen matrix seeded with the start cell.
Per level: harvest qualifying items, sort by (price, row, col), extend the result, breaking at k.
Build the next frontier from unvisited walkable neighbors.
Stop when the frontier empties or k items are collected; return them.
a.t: O(mn + Σ Lᵢ log Lᵢ) — every cell enters exactly one frontier, sorts shrink as levels widen, and selection halts at k items.

w: Always BFS first and rank second — recomputing distances per item or trusting DFS depth are the classic mistakes here. Remember the start cell itself qualifies when its price lies in range (distance 0), walls block movement but item cells never do, and ties must cascade through all four criteria, which is easiest via tuple comparison. For very large grids mention streaming the top-k with a size-k heap instead of a full sort. Likely follow-ups: dynamic prices requiring re-ranking, or multiple starting cells (multi-source BFS).
